blocks.text: The ¹³C NMR spectrum is simpler than ¹H NMR in which each peak (or signal) corresponds to a single, different environment or type of carbon atom. Chemical shift of each peak tells about its environment.

blocks.latex: \text{The number of peaks} = \text{The number of different carbon environments}
blocks.text_alt: The number of peaks = The number of different carbon environments

blocks.text: ¹³C NMR spectrum of ethane shows only one peak as both the carbon atoms have the same environment. In propane CH₃ – CH₂ – CH₃, there are two types of carbon environments, the two terminal -CH₃ carbons have the same environment while the middle -CH₂- carbon has a different environment. The ¹³C NMR spectrum of propane shows two peaks, one for the methyl carbon atoms while the other for -CH₂- carbon atom. Similarly, two peaks are observed in the ¹³C spectrum of ethanol (CH₃–CH₂–OH), due to the presence of two types of environments in this molecule (Figure 30.7).

blocks.alt: 13C NMR spectrum on a ppm scale from 60 to 0: a green line near 57 ppm, a pink line near 18 ppm and a line labelled TMS at 0. Inset: the displayed formula HO-C-C-H of ethanol with the carbon next to OH in green and the other carbon in pink.
blocks.caption: Figure 30.7: 13C NMR spectrum of ethanol (printed as 'Figure 30.3'; original drawing after the textbook's figure).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: This figure is printed with the caption number 'Figure 30.3'; the text calls it Figure 30.7.
Analyzing the ¹³C NMR spectrum of ethanol by using the data given in Table 30.3, it is evident that the peak at 18 ppm is for -CH₃ carbon, while the peak near 57 ppm is due to -CH₂- carbon atom.

There are two key differences between ¹H NMR and ¹³C NMR spectra. The relative peak area in ¹³C NMR is usually not proportional to the number of carbon atoms unlike ¹H NMR in which peak area shows the number of protons. Secondly, the peaks do not show splitting, hence these appear as vertical lines. Due to this, ¹³C NMR technique is less sensitive than ¹H NMR.
